title: Telecommunications
summary: Moving bits through noisy channels. Shannon capacity is the threshold: bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio set a hard ceiling on data rate, and every modulation and code is a way of approaching it.
sources: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

nodes.label: Decibels & Signal Power
nodes.summary: Power ratios on a log scale: +3 dB doubles, +10 dB is ten times; dBm references 1 mW.
nodes.outcome: Convert between power ratios, dB and dBm.
nodes.check: A signal goes from 1 mW to 100 mW. How many dB is that gain?

nodes.label: "Decibels add like watts"
nodes.summary: Two equal 10 dBm signals combine to 13 dBm, not 20 dBm: dB values multiply ratios, so adding powers needs linear units.
nodes.outcome: Add two powers given in dBm correctly.
nodes.check: Two equal, uncorrelated 10 dBm signals are combined. Total power?
nodes.answer: About 13 dBm (double the power is +3 dB).

nodes.label: Spectrum & Bandwidth
nodes.summary: Signals occupy frequency ranges; regulators allocate spectrum, and bandwidth is a scarce resource.
nodes.outcome: Read a spectrum plot and measure occupied bandwidth.
nodes.check: Why is radio spectrum licensed and auctioned?
nodes.answer: It is a finite shared resource; transmitters on the same frequencies in the same area interfere.

nodes.label: Noise & SNR
nodes.summary: Thermal noise sets a floor (kTB); signal-to-noise ratio decides how reliably symbols can be told apart.
nodes.outcome: Compute thermal noise power for a given bandwidth.
nodes.check: If you double the receiver bandwidth, what happens to thermal noise power?
nodes.answer: It doubles (+3 dB), because noise power is proportional to bandwidth.

nodes.label: Modulation: AM, FM, PSK, QAM
nodes.summary: Bits encoded in amplitude, frequency or phase; QAM packs more bits per symbol at the cost of noise margin.
nodes.outcome: Compute bits per symbol for an M-QAM scheme.
nodes.check: How many bits does each symbol carry in 64-QAM?

nodes.label: Shannon Capacity
nodes.summary: C = B log₂(1 + SNR): the maximum error-free rate of a noisy channel. No scheme beats it; good ones approach it.
nodes.outcome: Compute channel capacity and say which lever (bandwidth or SNR) helps more.
nodes.check: A 1 MHz channel has an SNR of 15 (linear). What is its Shannon capacity?

nodes.label: "Double the SNR, double the data rate"
nodes.summary: Capacity grows with the logarithm of SNR but linearly with bandwidth; doubling SNR adds only about one bit per second per hertz.
nodes.outcome: Compare the effect of doubling SNR with doubling bandwidth.
nodes.check: At high SNR, doubling the SNR increases capacity by roughly how much?
nodes.answer: About 1 bit/s per Hz of bandwidth; doubling bandwidth would double capacity.

nodes.label: Error-Correcting Codes
nodes.summary: Redundancy (Hamming, convolutional, LDPC, polar codes) lets receivers fix errors, trading rate for reliability.
nodes.outcome: Encode and correct a single-bit error with a Hamming(7,4) code.
nodes.check: A Hamming(7,4) code sends 7 bits for every 4 data bits. What can it correct?
nodes.answer: Any single-bit error in each 7-bit block.

nodes.label: Multiplexing & OFDM
nodes.summary: Sharing a medium by time, frequency or code; OFDM splits a wideband channel into many narrow orthogonal subcarriers.
nodes.outcome: Explain why OFDM handles multipath well.
nodes.check: Why does OFDM cope well with multipath echoes?
nodes.answer: Each narrow subcarrier has long symbols, so echoes smear only a small fraction of each symbol (plus a cyclic prefix absorbs them).

nodes.label: Antennas & Propagation
nodes.summary: Gain, path loss, fading and the link budget: will enough signal arrive above the noise?
nodes.outcome: Compute a link budget and its fade margin.
nodes.check: In free space, how does received power change if distance doubles?
nodes.answer: It drops to a quarter (−6 dB), the inverse-square law.

nodes.label: Optical Fibre
nodes.summary: Light guided by total internal reflection; attenuation and dispersion limit reach and rate.
nodes.outcome: Explain total internal reflection and modal dispersion.
nodes.check: What keeps light inside an optical fibre?
nodes.answer: Total internal reflection: the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding.

nodes.label: Packet Switching & Latency
nodes.summary: Store-and-forward networks: propagation, transmission, queuing and processing delays.
nodes.outcome: Compute end-to-end delay from its four components.
nodes.check: Light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s. What is the one-way propagation delay over 2,000 km?

nodes.label: Cellular Networks (4G/5G)
nodes.summary: Frequency reuse across cells, handover, scheduling and the trade-off between coverage and capacity (low vs high bands).
nodes.outcome: Explain why 5G millimetre-wave cells are small.
nodes.check: Why do 5G millimetre-wave cells cover much less area than low-band cells?
nodes.answer: High frequencies suffer greater path loss and are blocked by walls, foliage and even rain.

nodes.label: Software-Defined Radio
nodes.summary: Radio functions (filtering, demodulation) done in software on digitised samples.
nodes.outcome: Demodulate an FM broadcast with an SDR toolchain.
nodes.check: What hardware does an SDR still need before software takes over?
nodes.answer: An antenna, RF front end (amplifier, mixer) and an ADC to digitise the signal.
